To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in AD, there is an increase in the number of neuronal perikarya positive for Glu N1 and PSD- 95 and a decrease in the number of GluN2 A and GluN 2 B positive neuronal perikarya.
in the entorhinocortical areas of Alzheimer's disease, the NMDA receptor subunits and postsinaptic protein PSD-93 show an abnormal accumulation in the neuronal soma.

the NMDA receptor subunits GluN1 (NR1) and GluN3A (NR3A), the postsynaptic scaffolding protein PSD-95 and the presynaptic protein SNAP-25 are altered in AD, and that this is not the same in different cortical layers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of synaptic alterations in Alzheimer's disease (a disease that affects the synapse) and their possible consequences on neuronal network.
the study of the molecular basis of synaptic plasticity in AD and the development of novel strategies for the treatment of this devastating neurodegenerative disease.
the pathological modifications of synaptic proteins and receptors in Alzheimer's disease (Davoust et al., 2010).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the increase in NMDA subunit GluN1 is a pathological feature in AD and is correlated with the presence of neurodegeneration.
the NMDA receptor subunits and PSD95 are reorganized at the level of the perikarya and dendritic shafts in Alzheimer's disease, but not at the level of dendritic spines.

the NMDA receptor subunits and PSD95 expression are altered in AD, with a significant increase of GluN1 in the perikarya of neurons in the EC and FC and of GluN2 subunits in the neuropile of the EC and FC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the entorhinofrontal cortices, there are more NMDARs in the neuronal soma, but fewer in the neuropile, in AD compared with controls.

the synaptic changes in AD are not restricted to the neuropile but also affect the neuronal perikaryal compartment, and that these changes can be detected using the NMDA receptor and PSD-95 as markers.
the NMDA receptor subunits and PSD95 protein are re-organized in AD, and that the changes are more pronounced in the neuronal pericarya than in the neuropile.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NMDA receptor subunit GluN1 as well as PSD-95 protein accumulate in neuronal perikarya in AD.

the pathological reorganization of the NMDARs subunits and the postsynaptic protein, PSD-95, distribution in the entorinal cortex and frontal cortex of AD brains, may contribute to functional deterioration.
NMDA receptors are involved in the neurodegeneration process of the Alzheimer's disease and that they are good biomarkers for this disease.
